title: Week 14: Cloud Security Architecture, Shared Responsibility & AWS S3/IAM Lab
subject: Information Assurance and Security
description: Shared Responsibility Model (IaaS/PaaS/SaaS), IAM zero-trust evaluation, NHIs & STS, SCPs, KMS (Provider/CMK/HYOK), IMDSv2 vs. SSRF, CNAPP tooling (CSPM/CWPP/CIEM), and AWS S3/IAM lab.
sourceFile: BCS411L S2W14 Cloud Security Architecture.pdf, BCS411L S2W14 Lab Cloud Security Basics.pdf

questions.question: How does transitioning to public/hybrid cloud infrastructure alter the enterprise security perimeter compared to traditional on-premises data centers?
options: Cloud resources are provisioned via software-defined APIs, making the control plane and identity layer (IAM) the primary security perimeter rather than physical network firewalls
Cloud providers secure all customer data and IAM configurations so the customer has zero security duties
Physical data center switches remain solely managed by the cloud customer
Cloud infrastructure eliminates all APIs and runs only on static hardware cables
questions.answer: Cloud resources are provisioned via software-defined APIs, making the control plane and identity layer (IAM) the primary security perimeter rather than physical network firewalls
questions.explanation: Because anyone with valid API credentials can create, modify, or destroy cloud infrastructure over the internet, the control plane and identity layer become the primary security perimeter.

questions.question: In the Cloud Shared Responsibility Model, what is the distinction between 'Security OF the Cloud' and 'Security IN the Cloud'?
options: The Cloud Service Provider (CSP) is responsible for Security OF the Cloud (physical facilities, hardware, hypervisor); the Customer is responsible for Security IN the Cloud (data, IAM, configurations, guest OS/apps depending on model)
The Customer is responsible for Security OF the Cloud (data center guards); the CSP handles Security IN the Cloud (customer passwords and S3 bucket policies)
Security OF the Cloud applies only to SaaS; Security IN the Cloud applies only to On-Premises
Both terms mean the CSP absorbs 100% of regulatory liability for customer data breaches
questions.answer: The Cloud Service Provider (CSP) is responsible for Security OF the Cloud (physical facilities, hardware, hypervisor); the Customer is responsible for Security IN the Cloud (data, IAM, configurations, guest OS/apps depending on model)
questions.explanation: The CSP protects the underlying cloud infrastructure ('of the cloud'), while the customer secures what they put and configure inside it ('in the cloud').

questions.question: Across On-Premises, IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS models, which two layers ALWAYS remain the Customer's responsibility?
options: Customer Data & Content, and Identity & Access (IAM)
Physical Data Center, and Virtualization / Compute Hypervisor
Guest OS Patching, and Physical Network Switches
Application Logic, and Underlying Storage Hardware
questions.answer: Customer Data & Content, and Identity & Access (IAM)
questions.explanation: Even in SaaS (Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Google Workspace), the customer retains accountability for their data governance/DLP, user provisioning, MFA, and IAM.

questions.question: Under the Shared Responsibility Model, if an attacker exploits an unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability inside a customer's AWS EC2 instance (IaaS) to steal records from an attached S3 bucket, who is accountable?
options: The enterprise customer is accountable because under IaaS the customer owns guest OS/application patching, security groups, and IAM/S3 data protection
AWS (the CSP) is solely accountable for patching Apache Struts inside every customer EC2 VM
The customer's ISP is accountable for the unpatched Apache Struts library
Neither party is accountable because IaaS instances are exempt from patching
questions.answer: The enterprise customer is accountable because under IaaS the customer owns guest OS/application patching, security groups, and IAM/S3 data protection
questions.explanation: In IaaS (EC2/Azure VMs), the CSP secures hardware and hypervisor isolation, while the customer is fully responsible for guest OS/application patching, firewalls, IAM roles, and S3 access policies.

questions.question: How do responsibility boundaries shift from IaaS to PaaS (e.g., AWS RDS, Google Cloud Run) and SaaS (e.g., Microsoft 365)?
options: In PaaS, the CSP takes over OS/runtime patching and host availability while the customer secures apps, APIs, DB controls, and data; in SaaS, the CSP manages the full stack while the customer governs users, MFA, OAuth apps, and DLP
In PaaS, the customer manages physical server racks; in SaaS, the customer patches the hypervisor
In PaaS, IAM is managed solely by the CSP; in SaaS, there is no user authentication
IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS have identical customer responsibilities for OS patching
questions.answer: In PaaS, the CSP takes over OS/runtime patching and host availability while the customer secures apps, APIs, DB controls, and data; in SaaS, the CSP manages the full stack while the customer governs users, MFA, OAuth apps, and DLP
questions.explanation: As you move from IaaS -> PaaS -> SaaS, the CSP absorbs more infrastructure/OS/application management, but IAM and Data always remain with the customer.

questions.question: How do cloud IAM engines (AWS IAM, Azure RBAC, GCP IAM) evaluate an API request using deterministic zero-trust logic?
options: 1. Check for Explicit DENY (if yes -> DENIED, overriding all Allows) -> 2. Check for Explicit ALLOW (if yes -> GRANTED) -> 3. Otherwise DEFAULT IMPLICIT DENY (-> DENIED)
1. Default Implicit Allow -> 2. Check Explicit Allow -> 3. Ignore Explicit Deny
1. Explicit Allow overrides Explicit Deny -> 2. Default Implicit Allow
1. Evaluate MFA only -> 2. Grant admin access if the request comes from an EC2 instance
questions.answer: 1. Check for Explicit DENY (if yes -> DENIED, overriding all Allows) -> 2. Check for Explicit ALLOW (if yes -> GRANTED) -> 3. Otherwise DEFAULT IMPLICIT DENY (-> DENIED)
questions.explanation: Cloud IAM starts with Default Implicit Deny, grants access only on Explicit Allow, and enforces that any Explicit Deny (including SCPs or Permissions Boundaries) always overrides Allow.

questions.question: Why are Non-Human Identities (NHIs)—such as service accounts, IAM roles, CI/CD tokens, and AI agents—a critical cloud risk, and how should they authenticate instead of static keys?
options: NHIs vastly outnumber human users, and hardcoded static keys (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`) risk permanent leakage; best practice uses Temporary Security Credentials (STS), IAM Roles, and Workload Identity Federation expiring in 15–60 minutes
NHIs cannot be assigned IAM policies; they must always share the AWS root account password
Static API access keys automatically expire every 5 seconds, making STS unnecessary
Workload Identity Federation hardcodes plaintext secrets directly into public GitHub repositories
questions.answer: NHIs vastly outnumber human users, and hardcoded static keys (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`) risk permanent leakage; best practice uses Temporary Security Credentials (STS), IAM Roles, and Workload Identity Federation expiring in 15–60 minutes
questions.explanation: Eliminating long-lived static credentials in favor of short-lived STS tokens via IAM Roles and Workload Identity Federation drastically reduces the blast radius of credential leakage.

questions.question: What is the security function of Service Control Policies (SCPs) in a multi-account cloud organization?
options: Organization-wide guardrails applied at the root or OU level that cap the maximum permissions any account—even local account administrators—can exercise (e.g., blocking CloudTrail disablement)
Bucket-level encryption algorithms that replace TLS on port 443
Automated Nmap scripts that scan EC2 instances for vsftpd backdoors
Local firewall rules inside `/etc/iptables` on a Linux VM
questions.answer: Organization-wide guardrails applied at the root or OU level that cap the maximum permissions any account—even local account administrators—can exercise (e.g., blocking CloudTrail disablement)
questions.explanation: SCPs enforce non-bypassable organizational boundaries across member accounts so even local admins cannot disable CloudTrail logging or bypass S3 Block Public Access.

questions.question: Compare Provider-Managed Keys, Customer-Managed Keys (CMK), and Client-Side / Hold Your Own Key (HYOK) in cloud KMS architectures.
options: Provider-Managed: CSP controls/rotates keys (zero overhead, limited audit); CMK: Customer controls policies, rotation, and instant cryptographic erasure (PCI-DSS/HIPAA); HYOK: Customer encrypts locally and CSP never sees plaintext keys (sovereign/classified, disables server-side search)
Provider-Managed: disables server-side search; CMK: CSP never sees keys; HYOK: zero operational overhead
Provider-Managed: requires local C compilation; CMK: only for unencrypted public buckets; HYOK: managed entirely by AWS support
All three key models give the CSP full plaintext access and disable audit logging
questions.answer: Provider-Managed: CSP controls/rotates keys (zero overhead, limited audit); CMK: Customer controls policies, rotation, and instant cryptographic erasure (PCI-DSS/HIPAA); HYOK: Customer encrypts locally and CSP never sees plaintext keys (sovereign/classified, disables server-side search)
questions.explanation: KMS balances operational simplicity against control and compliance: Provider-Managed for general workloads, CMK for regulated enterprise data (PCI-DSS/HIPAA), and HYOK for sovereign/classified data.

questions.question: Why does enforcing IMDSv2 neutralize most Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) credential-theft attacks against `http://169.254.169.254` whereas traditional network firewalls fail?
options: Network firewalls allow traffic originating inside the compromised web app to reach the local link-local IP; IMDSv1 allows unauthenticated HTTP GET, whereas IMDSv2 requires an HTTP PUT with `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds` to obtain a session token
IMDSv2 moves the metadata endpoint from `169.254.169.254` to the public internet on port 8834
Network firewalls block all HTTP GET requests to port 80 globally
IMDSv2 encrypts EC2 hard drives with Client-Side HYOK keys
questions.answer: Network firewalls allow traffic originating inside the compromised web app to reach the local link-local IP; IMDSv1 allows unauthenticated HTTP GET, whereas IMDSv2 requires an HTTP PUT with `X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds` to obtain a session token
questions.explanation: SSRF originates from the legitimate VM itself, bypassing perimeter firewalls. IMDSv2 defeats simple SSRF and proxy forwarding by requiring a session-oriented PUT request + custom header before reading metadata.

questions.question: What is 'Configuration Drift & IaC Bypass' in cloud environments?
options: When infrastructure is initially deployed securely via IaC (Terraform, CloudFormation), but manual emergency edits in the web console silently reopen firewall ports or disable encryption
When virtual machines physically drift across data center racks
When an S3 bucket automatically enables all four Block Public Access checkboxes
When CI/CD pipelines enforce short-lived STS tokens instead of static keys
questions.answer: When infrastructure is initially deployed securely via IaC (Terraform, CloudFormation), but manual emergency edits in the web console silently reopen firewall ports or disable encryption
questions.explanation: Week 14 highlights three emerging cloud threat vectors: Insecure Interfaces & Shadow APIs, Configuration Drift & IaC Bypass, and Supply Chain & CI/CD Pipeline Compromise.

questions.topic: Cloud Security Tooling: CSPM, CWPP, CIEM
questions.question: Which descriptions correctly match CSPM, CWPP, and CIEM?
options: CSPM audits control-plane configs (public buckets, open SGs, disabled logging); CWPP protects runtime workloads (VMs, containers, K8s, serverless); CIEM analyzes complex IAM policies across human/NHI identities for over-privilege
CSPM protects container runtimes; CWPP audits Terraform files; CIEM blocks public S3 ACLs
CSPM is a malware disassembler; CWPP is a syslog shipper; CIEM is a disk imager
CSPM, CWPP, and CIEM are three AWS managed IAM policies for S3 read-only access
questions.answer: CSPM audits control-plane configs (public buckets, open SGs, disabled logging); CWPP protects runtime workloads (VMs, containers, K8s, serverless); CIEM analyzes complex IAM policies across human/NHI identities for over-privilege
questions.explanation: CSPM monitors control-plane posture against CIS/NIST benchmarks, CWPP secures compute workloads at runtime, and CIEM maps effective IAM entitlements and toxic permission combinations.

questions.question: How does a unified CNAPP reduce alert fatigue compared to standalone CSPM and CWPP scanners when prioritizing a public container with a medium CVE vs. an isolated internal VM with a high CVE?
options: CNAPP correlates CSPM, CWPP, CIEM, and IaC findings into a unified attack-path graph, elevating the internet-exposed container (especially if paired with an admin IAM role) above the isolated internal VM
CNAPP ignores all medium CVEs and only alerts on CVSS 10.0 findings
CNAPP automatically deletes every container that has any CVE
CNAPP disables CWPP runtime agents so fewer alerts reach the SOC
questions.answer: CNAPP correlates CSPM, CWPP, CIEM, and IaC findings into a unified attack-path graph, elevating the internet-exposed container (especially if paired with an admin IAM role) above the isolated internal VM
questions.explanation: By correlating network exposure, runtime vulnerability, and IAM blast radius into one graph, CNAPP prioritizes true toxic attack paths over isolated theoretical CVEs.

questions.question: According to the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) Top Threats to Cloud Computing 2026 report cited in Week 14, what ranks as the #1 security risk in enterprise cloud environments?
options: Inadequate Identity and Access Management (IAM)
Physical data center power outages
Outdated JPEG EXIF metadata libraries
Legacy Syslog over UDP port 514
questions.answer: Inadequate Identity and Access Management (IAM)
questions.explanation: Because cloud management is API-driven, inadequate Identity and Access Management (IAM) ranks as the #1 cloud security risk.

questions.question: In Part 2 of the Week 14 Cloud Security Basics lab, what recommended setting is kept under Object Ownership when creating the S3 bucket?
options: ACLs disabled (recommended)
ACLs enabled with Public Read/Write
Anonymous Guest Ownership
Legacy Root Account Static Keys
questions.answer: ACLs disabled (recommended)
questions.explanation: Step 2.1 creates a globally unique S3 bucket with `ACLs disabled (recommended)` and `Block all public access` enabled.

questions.topic: Lab: Four Layers of S3 Block Public Access
questions.question: Which four safeguards are activated when 'Block all public access' is enabled on an Amazon S3 bucket?
options: `BlockPublicAcls`, `IgnorePublicAcls`, `BlockPublicPolicy`, and `RestrictPublicBuckets`
`AllowPublicAcls`, `EnableHTTP`, `DisableTLS`, and `WildcardAction`
`DefaultDeny`, `ExplicitAllow`, `ExplicitDeny`, and `SCP`
`CSPM`, `CWPP`, `CIEM`, and `CNAPP`
questions.answer: `BlockPublicAcls`, `IgnorePublicAcls`, `BlockPublicPolicy`, and `RestrictPublicBuckets`
questions.explanation: The first two block/ignore legacy public ACL grants, while the latter two reject public JSON bucket policies and restrict access to authorized principals/AWS services.

questions.question: In Step 2.3 of the lab, what result confirms that `confidential_test.txt` is protected when pasting its S3 Object URL into an Incognito/Private browser window?
options: The browser returns an XML `AccessDenied` error
The browser downloads `confidential_test.txt` automatically
The browser redirects to `http://169.254.169.254`
The browser displays a Nessus PDF report
questions.answer: The browser returns an XML `AccessDenied` error
questions.explanation: An unauthenticated Incognito browser request triggers an XML `AccessDenied` response, proving S3 Block Public Access prevents unauthorized public exposure.

questions.topic: Lab: Bucket vs. Account Block Public Access
questions.question: Why do security benchmarks recommend enabling S3 Block Public Access at the AWS account level rather than solely at the individual bucket level?
options: Account-level Block Public Access applies globally across all existing and newly created buckets, preventing accidental exposure if a developer forgets to enable it on a new bucket or modifies one bucket's settings
Bucket-level Block Public Access only protects `.jpg` files, whereas Account-level protects `.txt` files
Account-level Block Public Access automatically deletes all IAM roles
Bucket-level settings expire after 15 minutes like STS tokens
questions.answer: Account-level Block Public Access applies globally across all existing and newly created buckets, preventing accidental exposure if a developer forgets to enable it on a new bucket or modifies one bucket's settings
questions.explanation: Account-level safeguards enforce a blanket safety net across every bucket in the account regardless of individual bucket creation errors.

questions.question: In Part 3 of the Week 14 lab, how is the IAM Role `IAS-Week14-ReadOnly-Role` configured for an EC2 instance?
options: Trusted entity type: `AWS service`, Use case / service principal: `ec2.amazonaws.com`, Permissions policy: `ReadOnlyAccess` (or `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess` for single-service production scoping)
Trusted entity type: `Public Internet`, Use case: `S3 Anonymous`, Permissions policy: `AdministratorAccess`
Trusted entity type: `IAM User`, Static keys stored in `/etc/passwd`, Permissions policy: `PowerUserAccess`
Trusted entity type: `External GitHub`, Permissions policy: `Action: * Resource: *`
questions.answer: Trusted entity type: `AWS service`, Use case / service principal: `ec2.amazonaws.com`, Permissions policy: `ReadOnlyAccess` (or `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess` for single-service production scoping)
questions.explanation: Steps 3.1–3.3 create `IAS-Week14-ReadOnly-Role` with trust principal `ec2.amazonaws.com` and attach `ReadOnlyAccess` (noting `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess` is stricter for S3-only needs).

questions.question: When inspecting the attached `ReadOnlyAccess` JSON policy in Step 3.3, which API action prefixes are permitted and which are excluded?
options: `Get*`, `List*`, and `Describe*` operations are permitted; `Put*`, `Create*`, and `Delete*` are excluded
`Put*` and `Delete*` are permitted; `Get*` and `List*` are excluded
`Action: *` and `Resource: *` are permitted for all services
`s3:PutObject` and `s3:DeleteBucket` are permitted
questions.answer: `Get*`, `List*`, and `Describe*` operations are permitted; `Put*`, `Create*`, and `Delete*` are excluded
questions.explanation: `ReadOnlyAccess` limits the assumed role to read/inspection calls (`Get*`, `List*`, `Describe*`), preventing modification or deletion.

questions.topic: Lab: IAM Role vs. Static Access Keys
questions.question: Why is attaching an IAM Role to an EC2 instance more secure than storing IAM User Access Keys (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`) in a server config file?
options: IAM Roles provide automatically rotated, short-lived temporary credentials via STS/IMDS instead of long-lived static secrets sitting on disk where file disclosure or git commits could leak them permanently
IAM Roles disable all networking on the EC2 instance
Static Access Keys only work in AWS Cloud Quest simulators and never in production
IAM Roles store plaintext passwords inside S3 public buckets instead of config files
questions.answer: IAM Roles provide automatically rotated, short-lived temporary credentials via STS/IMDS instead of long-lived static secrets sitting on disk where file disclosure or git commits could leak them permanently
questions.explanation: Eliminating static keys on disk prevents permanent credential theft if a config file, backup, or repo is compromised.

questions.topic: Lab: Risks of Broad Read-Only Access
questions.question: Although `ReadOnlyAccess` prevents modifying or deleting resources, what security risk arises if broad read-only permissions are granted unnecessarily across an entire cloud account?
options: An attacker who compromises the role can read sensitive S3 data, inspect DynamoDB tables, enumerate network/IAM configurations, and exfiltrate secrets or environment variables across every AWS service
It allows the role to delete S3 buckets using `s3:DeleteBucket`
It automatically converts the AWS account into an on-premises data center
There is zero risk because reading data can never cause a data breach
questions.answer: An attacker who compromises the role can read sensitive S3 data, inspect DynamoDB tables, enumerate network/IAM configurations, and exfiltrate secrets or environment variables across every AWS service
questions.explanation: Confidentiality breaches do not require write permissions. Broad `ReadOnlyAccess` violates Least Privilege—for S3-only workloads, `AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess` scoped to specific bucket ARNs should be used.

questions.question: How do best-practice IAM policies enforce Least Privilege instead of granting `"Action": "*", "Resource": "*"`?
options: By restricting permissions to exact API calls (e.g., `s3:GetObject`), specific resource ARNs, and contextual conditions (e.g., requiring MFA or restricting source VPC endpoints)
By granting `AdministratorAccess` and relying on users not to click delete
By disabling AWS CloudTrail so unauthorized actions are not logged
By sharing one root account across all microservices
questions.answer: By restricting permissions to exact API calls (e.g., `s3:GetObject`), specific resource ARNs, and contextual conditions (e.g., requiring MFA or restricting source VPC endpoints)
questions.explanation: Scoped permissions adhere to Least Privilege by pinning exact actions, target ARNs, and contextual conditions.

questions.question: Which two cloud threat vectors involve broken object-level authorization / unmonitored endpoints and compromised third-party container base images or build-server secrets?
options: Insecure Interfaces & Shadow APIs, and Supply Chain & CI/CD Pipeline Compromise
RAM Slack and NTFS `$MFT` Overwriting
TCP SYN Stealth Scans and OS Fingerprinting
Syslog UDP 514 Spoofing and Log Truncation
questions.answer: Insecure Interfaces & Shadow APIs, and Supply Chain & CI/CD Pipeline Compromise
questions.explanation: Modern cloud workloads face Shadow APIs/BOLA/broad OAuth scopes as well as compromised container images, open-source packages, and CI/CD pipelines.

questions.question: Which three overlapping access mechanisms can accidentally expose an object storage repository (like Amazon S3) if Block Public Access is not enabled?
options: Legacy Access Control Lists (ACLs), JSON Resource/Bucket Policies, and overly permissive IAM roles
Windows Prefetch, Shellbags, and LNK files
Nmap NSE scripts, Nessus plugins, and Wazuh decoders
CPU registers, RAM dumps, and hardware write-blockers
questions.answer: Legacy Access Control Lists (ACLs), JSON Resource/Bucket Policies, and overly permissive IAM roles
questions.explanation: Because ACLs, Bucket Policies, and IAM roles overlap, S3 Block Public Access acts as an overarching guardrail overriding public grants.

questions.question: Which KMS encryption model enables instant cryptographic erasure, customer-controlled key rotation, and strict audit governance for PCI-DSS or HIPAA enterprise workloads?
options: Customer-Managed Keys (CMK)
Provider-Managed Keys
Unencrypted Plaintext Storage
IMDSv1 Session Tokens
questions.answer: Customer-Managed Keys (CMK)
questions.explanation: CMKs allow customers to define key policies, rotate keys, audit usage, and immediately revoke keys for cryptographic erasure.

questions.question: What is a major operational trade-off of Client-Side / Hold Your Own Key (HYOK) encryption in cloud storage?
options: High computational and key-management complexity, plus it disables server-side search and indexing by the CSP
The CSP receives full plaintext copies of all encryption keys
It prevents customers from uploading files smaller than 4,096 bytes
It automatically makes all S3 buckets publicly readable
questions.answer: High computational and key-management complexity, plus it disables server-side search and indexing by the CSP
questions.explanation: Because data is encrypted locally before upload and the CSP never sees plaintext keys, cloud-side search/indexing features cannot inspect object contents.

questions.question: In the Week 14 lab prerequisites, what rule applies when using an AWS Free Tier account for daily tasks, and what zero-cost alternative is offered?
options: Log in as an administrative IAM user (avoid using the root account for daily lab tasks), or use the free AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner sandbox simulator
Always use the AWS root account with MFA disabled, or install Kali Linux on an S3 bucket
Share your credit card number and root keys in the lab report
Only use Google Cloud Run to configure Amazon S3 Block Public Access
questions.answer: Log in as an administrative IAM user (avoid using the root account for daily lab tasks), or use the free AWS Cloud Quest: Cloud Practitioner sandbox simulator
questions.explanation: The lab provides Option A (AWS Cloud Quest simulator, no credit card needed) and Option B (AWS Free Tier via an IAM user rather than the root account).

questions.question: In the Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP) diagram, what are the four pillars unified into one platform?
options: CSPM (Control Plane Posture), CIEM (Identity & Entitlements), CWPP (Runtime Workload Defense), and Shift-Left IaC & Supply Chain scanning
Nmap, Nessus, Wazuh, and Autopsy
CPU Cache, Physical RAM, Network Sockets, and Local Disk
Preparation, Detection, Containment, and Lessons Learned
questions.answer: CSPM (Control Plane Posture), CIEM (Identity & Entitlements), CWPP (Runtime Workload Defense), and Shift-Left IaC & Supply Chain scanning
questions.explanation: CNAPP unifies posture (CSPM), identity entitlements (CIEM), runtime workloads (CWPP), and pre-deployment IaC/container supply-chain scanning.

questions.question: In an IaaS environment (e.g., AWS EC2 or Azure Virtual Machines), which controls remain the customer's responsibility?
options: Guest OS patching, host-based firewalls, virtual network security groups, IAM policies, application logic, and data encryption
Physical data center perimeter guards and HVAC cooling
Underlying storage fabric hardware replacement and hypervisor isolation
Manufacturing server CPUs and memory DIMMs
questions.answer: Guest OS patching, host-based firewalls, virtual network security groups, IAM policies, application logic, and data encryption
questions.explanation: Under IaaS, the CSP stops at the hypervisor/virtualization layer; everything from the guest OS upward is secured by the customer.

questions.question: What does 'Shift-Left IaC & Supply Chain' scanning inside a CNAPP achieve before resources are deployed to production?
options: It scans Terraform/CloudFormation templates and container images directly in CI/CD pipelines to catch misconfigurations and vulnerable packages early
It shifts logs from the Hot Tier to the Frozen Glacier Tier
It moves IAM policies from Explicit Deny to Implicit Allow
It moves files from FAT32 to NTFS without changing cluster sizes
questions.answer: It scans Terraform/CloudFormation templates and container images directly in CI/CD pipelines to catch misconfigurations and vulnerable packages early
questions.explanation: Shift-left scanning catches insecure Terraform code and vulnerable container base images inside CI/CD before deployment.

questions.question: In the Lab's IAM Role Least-Privilege Architecture diagram, when an EC2 instance assumes `IAS-Week14-ReadOnly-Role`, which S3 operations are Allowed vs. Denied?
options: Allowed: Read/List (`s3:GetObject`, `s3:ListBucket`); Denied: Write/Delete (`s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteBucket`)
Allowed: Write/Delete (`s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteBucket`); Denied: Read/List (`s3:GetObject`)
Allowed: All actions (`s3:*`); Denied: None
Allowed: `ec2:TerminateInstances`; Denied: `s3:GetObject`
questions.answer: Allowed: Read/List (`s3:GetObject`, `s3:ListBucket`); Denied: Write/Delete (`s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteBucket`)
questions.explanation: The read-only role architecture permits read/list operations (`s3:GetObject`, `s3:ListBucket`) while implicitly denying mutating actions (`s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteBucket`).
